opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core idea is that no single safety measure is going to be sufficient on its own, and evaluations are a good example. Pre-deployment evaluations are incredibly valuable, but they have real limits. You're testing a system in a controlled setting, with a finite set of tasks, a finite amount of time, and a finite number of people trying to elicit capabilities. Once a model is out in the world, you have millions of users, lots of creativity, new scaffolding, new tools, and people combining the model with other systems in ways nobody anticipated. So there's almost always going to be some gap between what we measured and what the model can actually do.

Staged deployment is a way of acknowledging that gap and building a buffer around it. Rather than going straight from internal testing to a full, open release, you move through a sequence of steps. You might start with internal use, then trusted testers, then a limited API with monitoring and usage policies, and only later broader access, or in some cases releasing weights. At each stage you're widening the exposure a bit, but you keep the ability to observe what's happening and to pull back if something surprising shows up.

That's where the defence in depth comes in. If an evaluation misses a dangerous capability, say some uplift in a sensitive domain or an emergent ability to carry out longer autonomous tasks, a staged approach gives you more chances to catch it before it's irreversible. You've got monitoring on how the model is actually being used, you've got red teamers and external researchers probing it in the wild, you've got incident reporting channels, and you've got the ability to patch, add safeguards, restrict access, or roll back. Each layer catches some of what the previous layer let through.

I'd emphasise reversibility as the key property. A hosted model behind an API is something you can still adjust. Once weights are widely released, you've largely given up that option. So staged deployment is partly about sequencing decisions so the irreversible ones come last, after you've accumulated as much real-world evidence as you reasonably can.

It's not a panacea. Some harms could happen quickly, even in a limited release, and monitoring has its own blind spots, particularly around privacy and around misuse that's subtle or distributed. And there are competitive pressures that push labs to compress these stages. But as a principle, I think it's one of the more robust tools we have, precisely because it doesn't require us to be confident our evaluations are complete. It's designed for a world where we know we'll sometimes be wrong, and we want those errors to be detectable and correctable rather than catastrophic.

r001.rationale: The response describes widening access in stages and leaving irreversible decisions, such as broad weight release, until after more real-world evidence has been gathered.

r002.rationale: It says a hosted model can still be adjusted with safeguards or access restrictions if something surprising appears, while widely releasing weights largely gives up that option.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the starting point here is honesty about the limits of evaluations. Evaluations are incredibly valuable, and we invest a lot in them, but they're a sample. You're probing a model with a finite set of tasks, in a finite set of contexts, often before you fully understand what the model can do when it's combined with tools, or scaffolding, or when thousands of creative people start poking at it. There's a well-known phenomenon where capabilities get "elicited" months after release that nobody had found in pre-deployment testing. So if your whole safety story rested on "we evaluated it and it passed," that would be a fragile story.

Staged deployment is the response to that. The idea is that instead of a single moment where you go from zero exposure to full exposure, you move through a sequence of expanding contexts, and at each stage you're gathering information that you couldn't have gotten at the previous stage. So you start internally, with red teams and researchers. Then maybe a small set of external experts or trusted testers. Then a limited external release, perhaps with rate limits, monitoring, restricted modalities, no tool access. Then broader access. And crucially, each of those stages is a decision point, not just a milestone. You have criteria for what would make you pause, roll back, or add mitigations before going further.

The defence-in-depth framing is that these layers fail somewhat independently. Evaluations might miss a capability because you didn't think to test for it. But a staged rollout with good monitoring catches it because real usage surfaces things that structured evaluations don't. Even if monitoring is imperfect, the fact that access is still restricted at that stage limits the blast radius. And if something does get through, having the capacity to roll back or restrict is itself another layer. No single layer has to be perfect, which is the whole point of defence in depth. You're trying to make it so that a catastrophic outcome requires several things to go wrong at once, rather than just one.

I'd also say there's a kind of epistemic humility built in. The staged approach is a way of saying: we don't fully trust our own forecasts about what this system can do, and we're designing the process so that being wrong is survivable. That's a very different posture from "we've checked, it's fine, ship it."

The hard part, and I don't want to oversell this, is that it only works if you really are willing to stop. The commercial and competitive pressures all push toward treating each stage as a formality. So the governance question is how you make those decision points real, with pre-committed thresholds, with people empowered to say no, and ideally with some external visibility so it's not purely an internal judgment call. Staged deployment is a structure, but the structure is only as good as the institution's willingness to act on what it learns at each stage.

r001.rationale: The response describes expanding access in stages, limiting blast radius, and retaining the option to pause or roll back. It does not clearly identify avoiding irreversible proliferation of models with poorly understood capabilities as the purpose.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention keeping model weights unpublished or explain how doing so preserves the ability to change safeguards.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic idea is that you shouldn’t regard passing an evaluation as establishing that a system is safe. Evaluations give you evidence, but they can miss capabilities, or miss the circumstances in which a capability becomes dangerous. Staged deployment gives you another opportunity to discover those things before the consequences become very large.

So you might initially make a system available to a small number of users, with fairly constrained permissions and close monitoring. You’re looking at how it behaves in actual use, including how people combine it with tools or with other systems. If that reveals something unexpected, you have an opportunity to stop, investigate, and change the safeguards before expanding access.

But the staging has to be meaningful. A small number of users isn’t necessarily a small amount of risk if the system has extensive autonomy or access to sensitive infrastructure. And if you release the model weights, you may lose the ability to pull it back. So you want the initial deployment to limit the consequences of being wrong, as well as help you learn.

That’s the defence-in-depth aspect: evaluations, restrictions on what the system can do, monitoring, and the ability to intervene all provide different layers. None is perfect, but you don’t want a single missed capability in an evaluation to translate immediately into an irreversible, large-scale failure.

r001.rationale: The response says staged deployment lets you discover unknown risks before consequences become large, and warns that releasing model weights can make the system impossible to pull back.

r002.rationale: The response connects early discovery to changing safeguards before expanding access, and separately says released weights may be hard to pull back. It does not clearly state that keeping weights unpublished preserves the ability to change safeguards.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic idea is that we shouldn’t expect any set of evaluations to tell us everything we need to know about a model. Evaluations give you evidence, but there can be capabilities that you didn’t think to test for, or that only become apparent when people interact with the system in particular ways.

So instead of going straight from testing to making a model available to everyone, you expand access gradually. You might start with a small number of trusted users, with substantial monitoring and restrictions on what the system can do. That gives you another opportunity to discover unexpected capabilities or dangerous uses before the consequences are very large. And then, as you gain evidence, you can decide whether to expand access further.

The important thing is that these stages actually limit the potential harm. If you release the model weights, for example, you generally can’t reverse that decision. Whereas with controlled access, you have more ability to restrict use, investigate an incident, or stop deployment.

So staged deployment is an additional layer of defence, rather than a substitute for evaluations. And it has limits: if a capability could cause catastrophic harm even during a small deployment, you need stronger assurance before reaching that stage. But for risks that emerge through use, it can give you a valuable chance to notice and respond before scaling up.

r001.rationale: It recommends expanding access gradually and says releasing model weights is generally irreversible, allowing unexpected capabilities to be detected before wider deployment.

r002.rationale: It explains that controlled access preserves the ability to restrict use, investigate incidents, or stop deployment after unexpected capabilities emerge.
